topic.title: Deployment Architecture Overview
topic.shortdesc: A high-level overview of the on-premises deployment: the single-host container architecture, bundled technology stack, client tiers, and sizing guidance.

body.p: The solution is delivered as a self-contained Linux installer. The entire platform runs as containers on a single Linux host (a virtual machine or physical server that you control). The components communicate over an isolated internal network on that host, and only a small, well-defined set of ports is exposed externally. This topic describes the overall architecture and points to the topics that cover installation, configuration, and operation in detail.

section.title: Solution Architecture
section.p: All services run on a single Linux host. The web tier terminates HTTPS and proxies requests to the core platform services, which use bundled PostgreSQL and Redis instances. Outbound integrations are optional and can be disabled, so the deployment is capable of running fully air-gapped.

section.p: Users connect to through two client tiers:

dlentry.dd: The primary client for reviewers, authors, and administrators. The review UI runs in any modern web browser over HTTPS, so the end-user operating system is unconstrained.

The installed desktop application on author workstations connects to through its built-in Oxygen Content Fusion Connector add-on over HTTPS to submit documents for review and retrieve feedback. The desktop client is installed and licensed independently and runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

section.title: Technology Stack
section.p: All runtimes and infrastructure components below are bundled inside the delivered container images. You do not install or separately maintain a Java runtime, application server, or database on the host — only a supported operating system and a container engine are required.

row.entry: Docker containers on Linux, orchestrated with Docker Compose

section.note: A full inventory of bundled components and their versions (SBOM) is available on request for vulnerability scanning and compliance.

section.title: Supported Operating Systems
section.p: The server runs on a 64-bit Linux host with a supported container engine (Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 LTS, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, or CentOS 9). For the complete list of supported distributions, host prerequisites, and the installation procedure, see .

section.title: Hardware Sizing Guidance
section.p: The workload is driven primarily by publishing/validation batch jobs (CPU-intensive) and active review sessions (memory-intensive), more than by raw connection count. The baseline below runs the full set of services for a small team; scale up for higher concurrent load.

table.title: Sizing starting points by expected load

ul.li: Storage grows with the number and size of review repositories, document revisions, published outputs, and the search index. Provision generously and monitor it; an SSD is strongly recommended. For details about how storage is used and how to add more, see and .
Publishing is the heaviest CPU consumer; sites that publish large DITA maps frequently should favor more vCPUs.
For deployments that need more memory allocated to the services, see .
These are starting points. Final sizing should be confirmed with Oxygen based on your document volume and concurrency profile.

section.title: Network and Ports
section.p: TLS is terminated at the web tier. Inbound access is over HTTPS on port 443 (browsers, the desktop Author connector, and Web Author), with port 80 typically redirecting to HTTPS and port 9080 serving the administration console (restrict this to administrator networks). All other internal service ports (database, cache, application servers) are not exposed outside the host. For the authoritative list of incoming and outgoing connections, see . For the external services and endpoints that must be reachable when the corresponding features are enabled, see .

section.title: Authentication and Integrations
section.p: Authentication methods can be enabled individually or in combination and are configured through the administration console. Supported methods include built-in local accounts (email and password), LDAP / Active Directory (LDAPS), OIDC single sign-on (for example, Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, or Keycloak), and optional OAuth social login (Google, GitHub). LDAP/Active Directory or OIDC SSO are recommended for enterprise IT. Multi-factor authentication is not implemented in the application layer; enforce MFA at the identity provider when federating via OIDC or LDAP.
For configuration details, see the following topics:

ul.li: — single sign-on, email/password sign-up restrictions, LDAP settings, and account lockout.
— SMTP host/port for email notifications and password resets. Email is optional; if no mail server is configured, email-based features are disabled accordingly.

section.title: Backup, High Availability, and Dependencies
section.p: The appliance includes built-in backup tooling (shell scripts that save the backup locally). Integrate the backups into your organization's standard backup rotation and storage, and test restores periodically. For the backup and restore procedure, see .
The standard Enterprise appliance is a single-host deployment with no built-in active/active clustering. Use regular backups plus a documented restore procedure as the disaster-recovery strategy.

The deployment is self-contained by default and has no mandatory external or internet dependencies for core review functionality — it can run fully air-gapped. Optional external integrations (SMTP, LDAP/Active Directory, OIDC SSO, and Git servers) are the only services that communicate outside the host, and each can be turned off or pointed at internal equivalents. Updates are applied using the provided installation kit (new image versions); see .
